topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Comparing quantities
topic.scope: percentages, conversion, profit and loss, discount, simple and compound interest, tax

nodes.name: Percentage of a quantity and change
Profit or loss percent is on cost price
Profit = SP minus CP when SP > CP
SI = P×R×T/100 with T in years
Compound interest uses a growing principal
Half-yearly compounding halves rate, doubles periods
Tax is added on the price before tax

misconceptions.statement: Percent means the quantity is out of the number itself, so 25% means 25 items.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the % sign as a unit label like 'kg' instead of a ratio.
misconceptions.fix: Percent means 'per hundred', so 25% means 25 out of every 100, which is 1/4 of the whole.

probe.question: A class has 40 students and 25% are absent. How many are absent?

misconceptions.root_belief: a symbol is a label, not an operation

misconceptions.statement: The same percentage always means the same amount, so 10% of any quantity is the same.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the number 10 and forget that the whole changes.
misconceptions.fix: A percentage is a fraction of a whole, so 10% of 200 is 20 but 10% of 50 is 5.

probe.question: Is 20% of Ravi's marks the same as 20% of Sita's marks if Ravi scored out of 50 and Sita out of 200?

misconceptions.root_belief: a number means the same amount in every context
misconceptions.source_hint: research on proportional reasoning and percent as a relative quantity

misconceptions.statement: The higher percentage always means the larger quantity.
misconceptions.why: Students compare percent numbers without noticing the wholes are different.
misconceptions.fix: Percentages can only be compared by amount when the wholes are equal; 50% of 20 is less than 10% of 500.

probe.question: Which is more: 50% of 20 or 10% of 500?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger number means bigger effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on relative vs absolute comparison in percent problems

misconceptions.statement: To change a percent to a decimal you just put a decimal point in front, so 5% = 0.5.
misconceptions.why: Students remember 'move the point' but not how many places.
misconceptions.fix: Dividing by 100 moves the point two places left, so 5% = 5/100 = 0.05.

probe.question: Write 5% as a decimal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a procedure works without checking its meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student errors converting percent to decimal

misconceptions.statement: A percent like 1/2% is the same as 50%.
misconceptions.why: Students read 1/2% as the fraction one half and ignore the percent sign.
misconceptions.fix: 1/2% means half of one per hundred, which is 0.5/100 = 0.005, not 0.5.

probe.question: Write 1/2% as a decimal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a symbol can be ignored once read

misconceptions.statement: A fraction becomes a percent by just writing the numerator with a % sign, so 3/5 = 3%.
misconceptions.why: Students copy the top number and attach the symbol.
misconceptions.fix: Make the denominator 100 or multiply by 100: 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%.

probe.question: Express 3/5 as a percent.

misconceptions.root_belief: a procedure works without checking its meaning

misconceptions.statement: A percent can never be more than 100%.
misconceptions.why: Students think 100% is the whole and nothing can exceed the whole.
misconceptions.fix: A percent can exceed 100% when the quantity is more than the reference, e.g. 150% of 40 is 60.

probe.question: A price rose from 40 to 100. Can the increase be more than 100% of 40?

misconceptions.root_belief: a limit seen in examples is a universal limit
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student difficulties with percents greater than 100

misconceptions.statement: To find x% of a number, divide the number by x.
misconceptions.why: Students mix 'percent' with 'divide' and use 10% = divide by 10 for every x.
misconceptions.fix: x% of a number means multiply by x/100, so 20% of 80 is 80×20/100 = 16, not 80÷20.

probe.question: Find 20% of 80.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from one case works everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: research on percent calculation strategies, e.g. 'divide by the percent' errors

misconceptions.statement: Multiplying by a percent always makes the number smaller.
misconceptions.why: Students carry over 'multiplication makes bigger' reversed from fractions, or only meet percents below 100.
misconceptions.fix: Multiplying by a percent below 100 gives a smaller number, but above 100% gives a larger one.

probe.question: What is 120% of 50?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: If a price goes up 20% and then comes down 20%, it returns to the original price.
misconceptions.why: Students treat equal percentages as cancelling, ignoring that the base changes.
misconceptions.fix: The 20% decrease is on the new, bigger price, so the final price is 96% of the original.

probe.question: A price of 100 rises 20% then falls 20%. What is the final price?

misconceptions.root_belief: opposite operations always cancel exactly
misconceptions.source_hint: research on percent change and changing reference base

misconceptions.statement: Percent change is the difference divided by the new value.
misconceptions.why: Students use the larger or final number as the whole.
misconceptions.fix: Percent change is the difference divided by the ORIGINAL value, times 100.

probe.question: A value goes from 50 to 60. What is the percent increase?

misconceptions.root_belief: the larger number is always the whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on choosing the base in percent change problems

misconceptions.statement: Profit percent is calculated on the selling price.
misconceptions.why: Students use the price they see last, since the selling price is what the customer pays.
misconceptions.fix: Profit % = (profit / cost price) × 100, because cost price is the original amount invested.

probe.question: CP is 80 and SP is 100. What is the profit percent?

misconceptions.root_belief: the final number is always the whole
misconceptions.source_hint: research on base choice in profit and loss word problems

misconceptions.statement: A 10% profit and a 10% loss on the same item cancel out, so there is no overall gain or loss.
misconceptions.why: Students think equal percentages with opposite signs sum to zero.
misconceptions.fix: Each is calculated on a different cost price, so selling two items at the same price with 10% gain on one and 10% loss on the other gives an overall loss.

probe.question: One article sold at 10% profit and another at 10% loss, both at ₹990. Overall result?

misconceptions.root_belief: opposite operations always cancel exactly

misconceptions.statement: Profit is the selling price itself; the more you sell, the larger the profit.
misconceptions.why: Students equate earnings with profit and ignore the cost.
misconceptions.fix: Profit is selling price minus cost price; if SP is less than CP there is a loss.

probe.question: CP is ₹500, SP is ₹450. What is the profit?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Loss is found by subtracting the cost price from the selling price, even if SP is less than CP, and can be a negative profit amount without comparing.
misconceptions.why: Students always subtract in the same order, SP minus CP, without deciding gain or loss first.
misconceptions.fix: First compare SP and CP: if CP > SP, loss = CP − SP, a positive amount.

probe.question: CP ₹200, SP ₹150. What is the loss?

misconceptions.root_belief: always subtract the second from the first

misconceptions.statement: Discount percent is calculated on the selling price.
misconceptions.why: Students use the price they actually pay as the base.
misconceptions.fix: Discount is a percent of the marked (list) price; selling price = marked price − discount.

probe.question: Marked price ₹500 with 10% discount. What is the discount?
probe.wrong_answer: 10% of the price paid, which is unknown, so compute from 450 as ₹45

misconceptions.root_belief: the final number is always the whole

misconceptions.statement: Discount is the same thing as profit.
misconceptions.why: Both are amounts of money taken or kept in a sale, so students merge them.
misconceptions.fix: Discount is a reduction from marked price given to the buyer; profit is the shopkeeper's gain over cost price.

probe.question: An item with cost ₹100 has marked price ₹150 and is sold with a ₹20 discount. What is the discount?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Two successive discounts of 10% and 20% equal one discount of 30%.
misconceptions.why: Students add the percentages as if both were on the same base.
misconceptions.fix: The second discount applies to the reduced price, so 10% then 20% equals 28% overall.

probe.question: A shirt gets 10% off, then another 20% off. What single discount is this?

misconceptions.root_belief: percents on different bases can simply be added
misconceptions.source_hint: research on adding percentages with different bases

misconceptions.statement: In SI = P×R×T/100, time can be put in as months directly with a yearly rate.
misconceptions.why: Students plug in the number given without checking the unit.
misconceptions.fix: Rate is per year, so time must be in years; 6 months is 0.5 years.

probe.question: Find SI on ₹1000 at 10% per year for 6 months.

misconceptions.root_belief: units can be ignored when plugging numbers
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of unit errors in interest word problems

misconceptions.statement: Simple interest grows by a bigger amount each year.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up simple and compound interest, both described as 'interest grows'.
misconceptions.fix: In simple interest the same amount is added every year because it is always on the original principal.

probe.question: ₹1000 at 10% simple interest: interest in year 1 is ₹100. Interest in year 2?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: The interest is the amount you get back at the end.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse interest with total amount.
misconceptions.fix: Amount = principal + interest; the interest is only the extra money earned.

probe.question: P = ₹1000, interest = ₹200. What is the amount?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar sounding terms mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: Compound interest for 2 years is just twice the first year's interest.
misconceptions.why: Students extend the simple interest pattern by repeating the same step.
misconceptions.fix: In year 2 interest is on the new amount (principal plus year-1 interest), so it is bigger than year 1.

probe.question: ₹1000 at 10% compounded yearly: CI for 2 years?

misconceptions.root_belief: a repeated process adds the same amount each time
misconceptions.source_hint: research on linear vs exponential growth thinking

misconceptions.statement: Compound interest is calculated by (1+R/100) multiplied by T instead of raised to the power T.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the exponent as multiplication.
misconceptions.fix: Amount = P(1 + R/100)^T, which means multiplying the factor by itself T times.

probe.question: A = P(1+R/100)^T with P=1000, R=10, T=2. What is A?

misconceptions.root_belief: a power means repeated multiplication of the base by the exponent

misconceptions.statement: For half-yearly compounding you halve the rate but keep the time in years.
misconceptions.why: Students adjust only the rate and forget the number of periods.
misconceptions.fix: Halve the rate and double the number of periods: 2 years at 10% half-yearly is 4 periods at 5%.

probe.question: For 1 year at 10% compounded half-yearly, how many periods and what rate?

misconceptions.root_belief: a procedure works without checking its meaning

misconceptions.statement: Sales tax or GST is already inside the shown price and is never added on top.
misconceptions.why: Students think the marked price is always the final bill.
misconceptions.fix: If tax is charged extra, the bill is the price plus tax; for example 18% GST on ₹500 adds ₹90, giving ₹590.

probe.question: A bill is ₹500 before 18% GST. What do you pay?

misconceptions.root_belief: what is not shown does not exist

misconceptions.statement: To remove tax from a bill, subtract the tax percent of the total bill.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the percent to the final amount instead of the pre-tax price.
misconceptions.fix: Tax is a percent of the price before tax, so divide the bill by (1 + rate/100) to get the original price.

probe.question: A bill with 10% tax is ₹110. What was the price before tax?

misconceptions.root_belief: the final number is always the whole
